David Morales, officially an Army NCO and State Department employee, worked from the Havana embassy while David Phillips was a CIA contract agent there, and had served with Phillips in the 1954 Guatemala operation (PBSUCCESS). After the Bay of Pigs he ran the "secret war" penetration teams out of the JMWAVE station in Miami under Ted Shackley, with Rip Robertson among his team leaders, and supported William Harvey and John Roselli's Task Force W assassination efforts.

David Atlee Phillips began as a CIA contract agent and spent his career opposing Castro and communist influence in the hemisphere: Havana in 1959, propaganda for the Bay of Pigs, then covert action and counterintelligence in Mexico City (promoted in fall 1963), later chief of Cuban operations and of the Western Hemisphere Division. After retiring early he founded an association of former intelligence officers to counter criticism of the CIA, and wrote The Night Watch and a novel whose assassin character resembled David Morales.

Manuel Artime (AMBIDDY-1), an early anti-Castro leader of the MRR, met Senator Kennedy with other exile leaders in 1960. In 1963 he and Harry Ruiz Williams were chosen to lead a new, deniable "autonomous" offensive against Castro (CIA project AMWORLD), operating entirely outside the U.S. Newly released documents show the project was tightly compartmented even within the CIA.

That project was part of a broader multi-agency Kennedy administration effort to bring about a coup removing Fidel and Raúl Castro in favor of a provisional government with exile participation. The CIA supported rather than ran it, helping Artime build forces offshore and contacts in Latin America; Henry Hecksher and Carl Jenkins were key officers.

Antonio Veciana, a successful Havana accountant, broke with Castro and became an organizer and spokesman of Alpha 66. He says a secretive American directed much of the group's strategy and worked with him on several plots against Castro, one of which, in Chile, he likened to the Kennedy assassination.

John Roselli was a well-connected organized-crime "fixer" active in Hollywood, Las Vegas and Havana gambling, and a key organizer of the casino skim. When the CIA sought syndicate help to kill Castro, Roselli was recommended; he took part in attempts before and after the Bay of Pigs, the later ones under William Harvey. He relied on exile leader Tony Varona, who had ties to the Trafficante organization; Santo Trafficante Jr., who controlled much of the syndicate's Florida and Cuban business, had been jailed by Castro.

Among the exile groups most dangerous to Castro was Unidad Revolucionaria (UR), formed inside Cuba in 1960 from 27 groups at the initiative of the MRR's Rafael Díaz Hanscom. In early 1961 the CIA pledged it support, and by March thought it had penetrated Cuba's police and military and was planning uprisings. UR told the CIA it was not ready for military action, but was not warned of the Bay of Pigs invasion, and its network was devastated in the round-ups that followed.

JURE, founded by Manolo Ray, was social-democratic and seen by wealthier exiles and Batista-era politicians as "Castroism without Castro." CIA officers including Howard Hunt, Ted Shackley and David Morales distrusted Ray; one JMWAVE memo suspected JURE of spying on the station.

Gilberto Ugarte Alvarado, a Nicaraguan intelligence informant, told CIA officers in Mexico City he saw Oswald paid at the Cuban Embassy for an assassination. Local CIA officers, notably David Phillips, initially strongly backed the story.

John Martino, a Havana casino electrician who kept returning to Cuba after the revolution, was arrested and imprisoned for several years. After his release in late 1962 he published I Was Castro's Prisoner (1963), criticizing the State Department and naming people he knew, including David Morales.

Silvia Odio was the daughter of wealthy businessman Amador Odio; both her parents were imprisoned by Castro for aiding the resistance. She and her father were affiliated with Ray's JURE. She moved to Dallas in early 1963, stayed in touch with Ray and sought weapons sources for JURE; her younger sister, a Dallas college student, knew active DRE members.

Tony Cuesta, a former Havana businessman, became one of the most aggressive exile raiders, first with Alpha 66 and then Commandos L. A spring 1963 raid that sank the Soviet freighter Baku made him famous through Life magazine, whose photographer went along.

Operation Mongoose was the Kennedy administration's response to the Bay of Pigs, ordered in November 1961. Gen. Edward Lansdale led the planning, the CIA's part (Task Force W) was run by William Harvey from the JMWAVE station under Ted Shackley, and a senior group including Robert Kennedy oversaw it.

William Harvey headed Task Force W within Mongoose. Richard Helms had him revive the CIA–Roselli plot against Castro in 1962, apparently without the knowledge of the Kennedys or CIA Director McCone; several poisoning attempts followed. Harvey and Roselli stayed close in 1963 after Harvey was moved to Rome. Helms had also assigned Harvey to build an "executive action" capability, ZRRIFLE, to remove foreign leaders using criminal assets, which documents show remained active in 1963.

Alpha 66 was among the best-organized and most effective exile groups, raiding Cuban ports and Soviet shipping in 1962–63 and raising money among exile businessmen in New York and Puerto Rico. Antonio Veciana and Eloy Menoyo, a former Second Front of the Escambray leader, built it; Tony Cuesta and Eddie Bayo were its best-known raid leaders.

Tony Varona, acting head of the CIA-backed Cuban Revolutionary Council, led several exile parties and acted largely for former president Carlos Prío. The CRC worked with Interpen members on a camp near New Orleans in 1962 but dropped it under administration pressure. Varona's ties to the Trafficante organization led to his role in Roselli's poisoning attempts, for which he received arms, money and supplies.

Eddie Bayo (Eduardo Pérez) fought under Raúl Castro, then turned against him and joined the crew of the Tejana III, a former subchaser bought with King Ranch and exile money and fitted out by the CIA for supply runs before the Bay of Pigs. In 1963 the Tejana went to Artime's forces; Bayo became an aggressive Alpha 66 raid leader.
William Pawley is the subject of a 2012 biography by Anthony R. Carrozza.
Source: Mary Ferrell Foundation, CIA cryptonyms list.

William "Rip" Robertson, a CIA paramilitary officer, served with Morales in Guatemala, advised Brigade 2506 and led frogmen at the Bay of Pigs, then ran infiltration missions from JMWAVE. He and boat captain Eugenio Martínez reportedly took part in Harvey's unsanctioned missions during the Missile Crisis and the later TILT mission; he debriefed John Martino and later served in Angola and Vietnam.

Felipe Vidal Santiago, a former Cuban naval officer, kept John Martino informed on exile affairs and made several trips to Dallas in fall 1963. Distrustful of the CIA, he stayed independent, associated with Interpen and Roy Hargraves, and was among the first approached by Paulino Sierra when recruiting for the JGCE.

Alberto Fernández (AMDENIM-1), a Princeton graduate and former head of Cuba's sugar stabilization board, had raised money for Castro's movement before breaking with him. In exile he used business ties, including to the Klebergs of the King Ranch, to buy the subchaser Tejana in 1960 with Texan and Cuban money; Tony Cuesta and Eddie Bayo served in its crew. A 1958 FBI memo lists U.S. companies solicited for payments to Castro's rebels.
AMLASH was the CIA cryptonym for both a project and an individual, Dr. Rolando Cubela, who had led DRE fighters into Havana against Batista.

The Student Directorate (DRE) fought Batista, then was among the first to oppose Castro's turn to communism. Its network in Cuba was one of the most secure in 1962–63, and the CIA actively supported its Miami chapter. DRE members in New Orleans clashed with Oswald in 1963 and were among the first to tie him publicly to Castro after the assassination; the reports DRE sent its CIA case officer about Oswald remained withheld and were the subject of litigation as of 2006.

The CIA's AMTRUNK project sought Cuban military and political leaders willing to revolt, especially officers resentful of Soviet influence. AMTRUNK and AMLASH continued for years despite internal evidence that Cuban intelligence had compromised many assets, and concern that Cubela himself might be testing the CIA for Castro.

A document shows David Phillips searched the Mexico City station's photo files to check a claim by Pedro Gutiérrez Valencia that he saw an Oswald-like American at the Cuban Embassy on October 1, 1963, and reported the coverage was complete all day throughout September and October. That raises the question why the files held no photograph of Oswald entering or leaving.

This visit becomes a repeated reference in wiretapped calls by "Oswald" linking himself to a Soviet assassinations officer. When it was noted that the caller spoke poor Russian while Oswald was fluent, the CIA said the tapes had been routinely erased.

The station's translators were Mr. and Mrs. Tarasoff (named in Peter Dale Scott's Deep Politics II). Tarasoff said the station already knew Oswald's name before the October 1 call and was "very hot" about it.
Former FBI agent James Hosty said agent Michael DeGuire told him Oswald was under surveillance in Mexico City beyond the embassy visits and was photographed by a fountain.

CIA headquarters replied to Mexico City that its latest information on Oswald was his May 1962 return, although the officers who approved the reply, including Ann Egerter and Jane Roman of Angleton's counterintelligence staff and Thomas Karamessines, had read recent reports on his New Orleans FPCC activity. Shown the documents in the 1990s, Roman acknowledged she had signed off on something she knew was untrue.
Immigration and FBI staff in Mexico were later given full information and investigated, and this reached Hoover, but apparently not the U.S. field offices responsible for Oswald.

Records released later show the FBI had in 1962 turned an agent of Valeriy Kostikov, a German national codenamed TUMBLEWEED living in Oklahoma, who identified Kostikov as part of the KGB department responsible for sabotage and assassination. Hoover therefore knew the significance of any Kostikov contact. Evidence suggests Oswald made one visit to the Soviet Embassy, followed by recorded calls apparently placed from the Cuban Embassy on a day it was closed to the public.

Dallas FBI apparently was not told of the Kostikov contact, though the Bureau may have been monitoring the Oswald family. Kostikov was under daily surveillance as one of the most dangerous Soviet agents in the hemisphere, yet neither the FBI nor CIA questioned or specially watched Oswald in the following sixty days, though a year earlier he had been investigated merely for his subscriptions.

Oswald's FBI headquarters file held the Mexico City contacts, the follow-up and his New Orleans activity. Yet none of Hoover's many records from November 22–23 mentions a KGB contact; either the record was altered or Hoover chose not to share what he knew with the President, the Secret Service or the National Security Council.

By noon on November 23, CIA Mexico City cabled that it could not compare voices because the tapes had been erased, contradicting Anne Goodpasture's documents and the translator's account. Goodpasture later told the HSCA and the Review Board that tapes were compared and a copy taken to Texas, and the Review Board confirmed that two Warren Commission lawyers, Coleman and Slawson, listened to tapes in Mexico City. This suggests the station knew of the impersonation but did not share or confirm it.
The Mexico City tape episode typifies information in early FBI reports that later vanishes or changes as other agencies become involved.

Researcher Rex Bradford found that only the recording of Hoover's November 23 call to Johnson appears to have been erased, a fourteen-minute gap, though a transcript survives. Soon after, a Belmont memo to Tolson confirmed Dallas agents had heard the tape. The FBI also held an intercepted Oswald letter to the Soviet Embassy mentioning "comrade Kostin."

Hoover eventually had to accept the CIA's position that no such tape existed. In January 1964 he warned his staff about trusting the CIA, writing that he could not forget its "false story re: Oswald's trip to Mexico City."

Bernardo de Torres, a Bay of Pigs veteran held by Castro until December 1962, became intelligence chief of the reconstituted Brigade 2506, knew Interpen members, and later figured in the Garrison investigation. Roy Hargraves, an American active in exile operations with Gerry Patrick Hemming's Interpen, trained members of Sánchez Arango's AAA group and, per FBI records, led a 1963 raid into Cuba funded by Rolando Masferrer.
